canvas-01.description: This part is the map block printed in the lower left corner of Sheet 1, the title and index sheet of the atlas, inside a heavy border below the key map. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north at the top, and shows blocks 55 and 56 on the east side of North Main Street between Jefferson Street at the top and Delavan Street at the bottom, with North Franklin Street running north to south through the middle; on the key map these blocks lie between Sheets 4 and 7 at the north end of the business district. Block 55, between North Main and North Franklin Streets, is lined on North Main Street with two-storey brick and frame dwellings, several in attached pairs, and has a row of three brick double houses on Delavan Street; stables and auto garages stand at the backs of the lots. Block 56, east of North Franklin Street, holds frame dwellings along the street and, at its north end, the McGinness and Cole express service and public warehouse with its sheds. The area north of the blocks is open and labelled Base Ball Grounds, and the east side of block 56 is marked Steep Hillside. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches and two hydrants are drawn in the streets. The sheet's scale bar is printed in the middle of North Main Street, and the rest of Sheet 1 (key map, notes on the water supply and fire department, and the street and specials index) is left out of this part.
notes: Delavan is today Delevan Street; North Main, North Franklin and Jefferson are North Main Street, North Franklin Street and Jefferson Street.
The specials index spells the warehouse firm McGinnes & Cole; the map prints McGinness & Cole.
Placed from three points (two detected, Jefferson Street / North Main Street hand-picked because the scale bar is printed in North Main Street): an exact first-order fit with no check.

Printed sheet 1: key map (about 550 ft to an inch), water and fire notes, street and specials index; bottom left a 50 ft map block (blocks 55, 56: N. Main, N. Franklin, Delavan, Jefferson St.) between the key map sheets 4 and 7. One part to configure (the bottom-left map); the key and index are not mapped.

sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 covers the north end of Lambertville, from Cherry Lane at the top to Elm Street at the bottom, and from the Delaware and Raritan Canal and the Belvidere Division of the Pennsylvania Railroad on the west to North Main Street on the east. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and carries a compass rose near the centre. North Union Street runs the length of the sheet. West of it, between the street and the railroad tracks, stands the Lambertville Pottery Company, a large plant of numbered buildings with saggar-drying rooms, kilns, a packing and crate shop, a casting house, an office and a slip house, with a coal trestle running behind it. South of the pottery are Smith and Sons Corporation, manufacturers of wire goods, an auto storage building, and a row of attached two-storey dwellings along North Union Street down to Elm Street. At the southwest corner the New Jersey Power and Light Company power station is marked as used in emergency. East of North Union Street the F. A. Woodward Company canning factory and chicken hatchery occupies the large block north of Elm Street, with warehouses, corn cribs and a shipping platform, and frame houses face Elm Street. Between Cherry Lane and Arnett Avenue there is a row of nine frame dwellings on lots facing North Union Street, and open ground fills most of the block east of them. Arnett Avenue is marked not improved. Along North Main Street on the east edge stand pairs of houses and the Mt. Carmel Baptist Church (colored). A band along the east margin is marked vacant.
notes: Cherry Lane is Cherry Street today; Arnett Av. is Arnett Avenue; Elm is Elm Street.
Arnett Avenue is lettered NOT IMPROVED on this sheet.
The sheet is drawn with the street grid turned about 15 degrees from north in the fit, although the compass rose is drawn upright on the sheet.
North Main Street is drawn only as its west edge with the legend VACANT BEYOND along the east margin; Cherry / North Main was left out of the fit (narrow pair, 3.6 m residual).

North end: Cherry Lane, Arnett Av., Elm, N. Union, N. Main, Delaware & Raritan Canal and Belvidere Division R.R.; Lambertville Pottery, power house, Woodward canning factory. 50 ft. 5 points; Cherry Lane / N. Main excluded (only the west edge of N. Main drawn).

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 covers six blocks of north Lambertville between Elm Street at the top and Delaware Avenue at the bottom, from the Delaware and Raritan Canal on the west to North Main Street on the east, with Clinton Street, North Union Street and George Street running north to south and Buttonwood Street and Perry Street running east to west. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north at the top. The northwest block, between the canal and North Union Street, is the most commercial: C. A. Niece's lumber, coal and feed yard with a feed mill (power and light by electricity), lumber sheds, a feed warehouse and supplies building, J. L. Fields and Son's coal and ice yard with an ice house and a poultry building, and two railroad switch tracks curving off the Pennsylvania Railroad along the canal into the yards. The Columbia Chemical Company No. 4 fire house stands on North Union Street at the south end of that block. The rest of the sheet is residential: rows of two- and three-storey frame and brick dwellings, many in attached pairs, with stables and auto garages at the backs of the lots. The 3rd Ward School, a brick building heated by steam, occupies the North Main Street end of the block between Buttonwood and Perry Streets. A garage with a concrete incline stands at Elm and North Union Streets. Water pipes of 4 and 6 inches are drawn along every street, with hydrants marked. East of North Main Street the sheet is left blank, and the block south of Delaware Avenue belongs to Sheet 4.
notes: Elm, Buttonwood, Perry, Clinton and George are printed without a suffix; today they are Elm Street, Buttonwood Street, Perry Street, Clinton Street and George Street.
Two Pennsylvania Railroad switch tracks enter C. A. Niece's and J. L. Fields and Son's yards from the canal side.
Elm to Delaware Av., canal to N. Main (Clinton, N. Union, George). 50 ft, north up. Pilot sheet.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 shows the residential and institutional heart of north-central Lambertville: sixteen blocks in a four-by-four grid bounded by Delaware Avenue at the top, York Street at the bottom, the Delaware and Raritan Canal on the west and North Main Street on the east. Clinton Street, North Union Street, George Street and North Main Street run north to south, crossed by Delaware Avenue, Jefferson Street, Delavan Street and York Street. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with a compass rose at the left margin. Almost every block is lined with two- and three-storey frame and brick dwellings, many of them paired, with stables and small outbuildings at the back of the lots. A narrow strip west of Clinton Street between the street and the canal holds a row of houses on deep lots. Larisons Alley crosses the block between Delaware Avenue and Jefferson Street east of George Street. Two institutions stand out: the Centenary M. E. Church, heated by steam with gas and electric light, in the block between Jefferson and Delavan Streets west of George Street, and St. Andrews Episcopal Church with its Parish House at the York Street end of the block east of George Street. A second church building with a tower stands in the block between North Union and George Streets near York Street. At the southwest corner, south of Delavan Street, the canal side holds an auto sales building and garage with auto stalls, and an undertaker's storage and auto house. Printed block numbers 12 to 20 appear on the sheet, and adjoining sheets 3, 5, 6, 7 and 1 are marked at the edges.
notes: Delavan is Delevan Street today; the other sheets of the atlas print both Delavan and Delevan.
Clinton, George, Jefferson and York are printed without a suffix; today they are Clinton Street, George Street, Jefferson Street and York Street.
George / York was rejected by the fit at 6.7 m; the other 15 junctions fit within 1 m RMSE.
Delaware Av. to York, canal to N. Main (Clinton, N. Union, George; Jefferson, Delavan). 50 ft.

sheet-5-1.description: The left half of Sheet 5 shows the strip of Lambertville between the Delaware River and the Delaware and Raritan Canal from Delavan Street at the top to Bridge Street at the bottom, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north at the top. A heavy vertical line divides it from the right half of the sheet, which continues the same strip south of Bridge Street. The Belvidere Division of the Pennsylvania Railroad runs along the west bank of the canal. The north half is taken up by the New Jersey Rubber Company's works: a new process building, storage and devulcanizing buildings, drying, mixing and machine rooms, a cook house, a carpenter's shop, resin and oil storage, and a large stock house and cutting building, with automatic sprinklers throughout and a long note on its watchman, power, heat and water supply. South of the works, Lambert Street runs along the river side with frame dwellings, a boat house and storage sheds, and Coryell Street crosses the canal on a draw bridge. Further south the Head Race leaves the canal to Joseph G. Lear's flour mill (closed), with a warehouse, the Hunterdon Laundry Company, wagon houses and dwellings on Lambert Street, and at the foot of the sheet the Elks Home and the Treftz House on Bridge Street beside the iron bridge to New Hope, Pennsylvania. A narrow strip east of the canal shows the edges of blocks drawn on Sheets 4 and 6, with York Street and Delavan Street.
notes: Lambert is today Lambert Lane, which ends at Coryell Street; the stretch of Lambert north of Coryell, along the rubber works, is gone. Delavan is today Delevan Street.
Lambert is drawn offset at Coryell (the north stretch about 40 ft east of the south stretch), joined by a narrow lane.

Placed from one detected junction (Bridge Street / Lambert Lane) at the atlas scale (7.85 px/ft) with rotation from its measured lines; a hand pick at Coryell Street / Lambert Lane gave a scale 12 percent off and was not used.
Belvidere Division of the Pennsylvania Railroad along the canal; today the Delaware River Heritage Trail.

Riverfront west of the canal, two parts side by side divided by a heavy vertical line: left (part 1) Delavan St. to Bridge (New Jersey Rubber Co., Lambert, Coryell, Lear flour mill); right (part 2) south of Bridge (PRR passenger station, freight house, shops, Ferry St. at the edge). 50 ft, north up.

sheet-5-2.description: The right half of Sheet 5 continues the strip between the Delaware River and the Delaware and Raritan Canal south of Bridge Street, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north at the top and divided from the left half of the sheet by a heavy vertical line. Bridge Street crosses the top of the part, with the iron bridge to New Hope, Pennsylvania at the river end, a draw bridge over the canal at the other, and the foot of Lambert Street to the north. Below it lie the railroad grounds of the Belvidere Division of the Pennsylvania Railroad: the brick passenger station, an express office, two long frame freight houses with a platform, a water tank on an 8-inch pipe, a tool house and a supervisor's office, and several sidings and a switch fanning out along the canal bank. Geo. W. Massey's coal yard stands beside the river with a coal shed, a fertilizer store and a curved coal trestle. At the foot of the part are the Pennsylvania Railroad shops (print shop and storage, blacksmith shop and carpenter shop), noted as having no power, with stove heat and electric lights, and a cement store. The rest of the strip is open ground, marked no exposure toward the river. Ferry Street meets the canal at the right edge, and the edges of blocks on Sheets 6 and 8 are drawn beyond the canal.
notes: Lambert Street is today Lambert Lane.
Placed from one detected junction (Bridge Street / Lambert Lane, at the top edge) at the atlas scale (7.85 px/ft) with rotation from its measured lines: low confidence away from Bridge Street.
Belvidere Division of the Pennsylvania Railroad; the line is today the Delaware River Heritage Trail.

Riverfront west of the canal, two parts side by side divided by a heavy vertical line: left (part 1) Delavan St. to Bridge (New Jersey Rubber Co., Lambert, Coryell, Lear flour mill); right (part 2) south of Bridge (PRR passenger station, freight house, shops, Ferry St. at the edge). 50 ft, north up.

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 is the commercial centre of Lambertville. It covers eight blocks in the middle of town between York Street at the top and Ferry Street at the bottom, from the Delaware and Raritan Canal on the west to North and South Main Streets on the east. North and South Union Street, George Street and Main Street run north to south; York, Coryell, Church, Bridge and Ferry Streets cross them. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with a compass rose at the left margin. Two draw bridges cross the canal at the ends of Coryell Street and Bridge Street. The densest blocks lie around Church and Bridge Streets, with brick stores and offices, the Strand Theatre (moving pictures), the post office, the Odd Fellows Hall, the Masonic Hall, a library, a bank, a drug store, the Belmont Hotel, W. A. Hall's feed mill, livery and boarding stables, a garage and a hall at South Main Street, and the Presbyterian Church. St. John's Roman Catholic Church, its Parochial School and the sisters' house occupy the block between George Street and Main Street south of Church Street, and the First Baptist Church stands south of Bridge Street. The Lambertville House stands at the corner of Union and Bridge Streets. In the block north of Coryell Street, east of George Street, is a park with a soldiers' monument, a band stand and a club, next to the jail. Printed block numbers 24, 25, 26, 31, 32, 34 and 35 appear, with Jos. Finkle's junk yard, the Kooker Sausage Company and the Record printing office on the west side near the canal. Blackwell Court runs between Church and Bridge Streets.
notes: Lilly Street is Lily Street in OpenStreetMap.
Coryell, Church, Bridge, Ferry and York are printed without a suffix; today they are Coryell Street, Church Street, Bridge Street, Ferry Street and York Street.
George Street was left out of the fit: its two junctions (with Coryell and with Church) were 10 to 12 m from the drawn ones, so the modern line looks displaced from the drawn street.
Union Ho. (the Union House hotel) is lettered at the lower left; a street west of South Union Street is marked NOT NAMED.
Downtown: York to Ferry, canal to N./S. Main (Union, George, Coryell, Church, Bridge). 50 ft. George Street left out (junctions with Coryell and Church 10 to 12 m off).

sheet-7-1.description: The main part of Sheet 7 covers the east side of central Lambertville from Delevan Street at the top to Bridge Street at the bottom, between North Main Street on the west and the hillside east of Washington Street, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north at the top. York, Coryell and Church Streets cross North Main and North Franklin Streets in a regular grid of blocks 36 to 42; McCready's Alley runs through the block south of Church Street, and Grants Alley through the block east of North Franklin Street. North Main Street is lined with brick stores and dwellings, many with stores on the ground floor; the Franklin Hotel stands on North Franklin Street near Bridge Street, Geo. C. Green's general machine shop on York Street, the Fleetwing Hook and Ladder Company No. 3 fire house and a twelve-car garage on Church Street, and a Standard Oil tank wagon shed on Delevan Street. The rest is frame dwellings with stables and garages. East of North Franklin Street the ground rises steeply: Rock Cliff and Steep Hillside are lettered along the slope, Washington Street climbs north past School Hill to meet York Street and York Road, and Hancock Street branches off to the northeast. The Lambertville High School stands alone on the hill in block 77. A heavy line cuts off the lower right corner, which holds a separate part of the sheet (North Union Street at Cherry Lane, at the north end of town).
notes: Delevan is printed with this spelling here (the index and Sheet 1 print Delavan); today Delevan Street. York Road is today the north end of York Street.
McCready's Alley appears in OpenStreetMap as McCreedys Alley (a service road); Grants Alley is a service road.
Washington Street / York Street was left out: the modern junction lies where York Road leaves Washington Street, which the sheet does not draw the same way.
The fitted scale (7.53 px/ft) is about 4 percent below Sheet 3's (7.85 px/ft); the north-south spacing of York, Coryell and Church Streets is drawn short.

East of N. Main from Delevan to Bridge (N. Franklin, Washington, York Rd., Hancock, Coryell, Church, McCready's Alley): part 1. A heavy line cuts off part 2 at the lower right: N. Union north of Cherry Lane, at the north end of town. 50 ft, north up.

sheet-7-2.description: This part is the lower right corner of Sheet 7, cut off from the rest of the sheet by a heavy line, and shows a separate area at the north end of Lambertville: North Union Street north of Cherry Lane, beyond the top of Sheet 2. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with its own north arrow pointing up. North Union Street runs up the part with frame and brick dwellings on its west side and, on its east side, a row of attached two-storey frame dwellings at the corner of Cherry Lane, with a note of a small auto house beyond; block 78 lies behind them. West of North Union Street, the tracks of the Pennsylvania Railroad (Belvidere Division) run north in a group of four lines with a switch, and a stone dwelling stands beyond them with a note that the freight auto house is 160 feet away. Most of the area toward the railroad is open ground marked no exposure. Cherry Lane enters at the bottom edge, with a hydrant and a 6-inch water pipe at the corner.
notes: Cherry Lane is today Cherry Street.
Placed from one detected junction (Cherry Street / North Union Street) at the scale of the sheet's main part (7.53 px/ft), with rotation from its measured lines: low confidence away from the corner.
The Pennsylvania Railroad line here is abandoned today (Delaware River Heritage Trail).

East of N. Main from Delevan to Bridge (N. Franklin, Washington, York Rd., Hancock, Coryell, Church, McCready's Alley): part 1. A heavy line cuts off part 2 at the lower right: N. Union north of Cherry Lane, at the north end of town. 50 ft, north up.

sheet-8-1.description: Part 1 is the main map of Sheet 8 and shows the south side of Lambertville between Ferry Street and the Delaware and Raritan Canal. The sheet is turned on the page, so that north lies to the left and the streets that run east to west today appear vertical: Ferry Street and Lilly Street at the left edge, Swan Street in the middle and Mt. Hope Street at the right, crossed by South Main Street (running diagonally), Wilson Street and South Union Street near the bottom. South Franklin Street cuts across the top of the sheet and Brunswick Avenue is lettered at the head. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the compass rose turned to match. A creek runs from top to bottom between Lilly Street and Swan Street, spanned by bridges at South Main Street and South Union Street, and the canal and its towpath form the bottom edge, with the Belvidere Division of the Pennsylvania Railroad below. Rows of attached two-storey frame and brick dwellings line Swan and Wilson Streets, with the 1st Ward School, heated by steam without light, on Wilson Street. Industry stands at the creek: the Lambertville Gas Company (not operated), a fire department house for the Hibernian Engine Company No. 2, storage for the Lambertville Rubber Company, L. T. Kugler's machine shop, and the Jespersen News Print Company's large plant, closed and entirely vacant, beside the canal. McDermott Bros. coal yard, closed, is at the lower right. A heavy line cuts off the upper right corner, where a separate inset shows buildings of the Delaware and Raritan Canal Company (part 2).
notes: Lilly is Lily Street today; Mt. Hope is Mount Hope Street; Charlevoix Pl. is not in the OpenStreetMap extract.
Charlevoix Place is lettered ARBITRARY along the canal edge; a street marked NOT NAMED lies west of Ferry Street.
The sheet is turned: the fit gives a rotation of about -71 degrees (north to the left).
The creek is lettered only as Creek.

South of Ferry/Bridge, turned (north to the left, rotation about -71): S. Main, S. Union, S. Franklin, Swan, Wilson, Mt. Hope, Lilly, Charlevoix Place, canal. Part 1 placed; part 2 is an inset in the upper right behind a heavy line (Delaware & Raritan Canal Co. buildings, block 93), unplaced. 50 ft.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Delaware & Raritan Canal Co. buildings, block 93 (upper right, behind a heavy line) (no street junction; needs step 6b: a point carried from sheet-9 or parcel corners).

sheet-9-1.description: The left part of Sheet 9 shows the northern stretch of South Main Street at the south end of Lambertville, from Mount Hope Street at the top to below Feeder Street, between the Delaware and Raritan Canal feeder basin on the west and a steep hillside on the east. It is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with its north arrow turned to the left of the page, and a heavy line divides it from the right part of the sheet, which continues South Main Street further south. Wilson Street meets Mount Hope Street at the top. The large block between Mount Hope and Feeder Streets is mostly open ground, with the Lambertville Iron and Steel Company's foundry at its west corner beside the Basin. South Main Street is lined on both sides with two- and three-storey frame, brick and stone dwellings, house numbers 102 to 202. South of Feeder Street lie a Lambertville Rubber Company warehouse and, between the Head Race and the Tail Race at the foot of the part, the William Mann Company paper mill: beaters, rotary and cutting rooms, machine room, finishing room, carpenter's shop and stock storage, with a note on its watchman, power and fire pumps. A strip of steep hillside and the scale of feet lie between South Main Street and the dividing line. A boxed inset at the bottom centre (the Lambertville Rubber Company's box shop and sheds on South Main Street) is not part of this part.
notes: Mount Hope is today Mount Hope Street; Feeder is today Feeder Street, a short stub off South Main Street; Wilson Street today continues south of Mount Hope Street, which the sheet does not draw.

Placed from Mount Hope Street / South Main Street (detected) and a point derived 300 ft down the drawn South Main Street on the bearing of the modern street, at the atlas scale (7.85 px/ft): low confidence.

At that scale the drawn Feeder Street lies about 28 m south of the modern Feeder Street junction, and Wilson Street about 6 m too far from South Main Street; either the sheet is drawn about 12 to 17 percent larger than 50 ft to an inch here, or those streets have moved. Not resolved.
The fitted rotation (-4.7 degrees) differs by about 19 degrees from the neighbouring sheets: the sheet is turned on the page to follow South Main Street.

South end along South Main Street. Three parts: part 1 (left of a heavy vertical line) Mt. Hope to below Feeder (Lambertville Iron & Steel foundry, Wm. Mann Co. paper mill); part 2 (right) South Main at Weeden (W. H. Gandey paper mill, Lambertville Rubber Co.); part 3 boxed inset at the bottom (Lambertville Rubber Co. sheds), unplaced. 50 ft; the sheet is turned about 19 degrees from its neighbours.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: boxed inset: Lambertville Rubber Co. box shop, shook storage and scrap sheds on South Main Street (turned, north up-left) (no street junction; only South Main Street is drawn; needs parcel corners (locate.py corner) or a point carried from a neighbouring sheet).

sheet-9-2.description: The right part of Sheet 9 continues South Main Street south from the foot of the left part, at the south end of Lambertville, drawn at 50 feet to an inch and divided from the left part by a heavy vertical line. The Tail Race and the Head Race of the mills run down the west side, with a coal yard at the top. South Main Street runs down the middle of the part; Weeden Street branches off it to the southeast past frame and brick dwellings, and a brook crosses the southeast corner below a steep hillside. W. H. Gandey's paper mill stands between the Head Race and South Main Street, with its finish room, machine room, beaters and stock rooms, a note on its watchman, power and lighting, and a coal heap and twelve-inch suction pipe to the race. The south half of the part is filled by the works of the Lambertville Rubber Company: shoe making, drying, curing, compounding and vulcanizing rooms, a calendering and cutting building, heel and boot making, storage and boot shops, a printing shop and a packing and shipping building on the east side of South Main Street, with automatic sprinklers and a long note on its fire protection. The east side of South Main Street north of the works has dwellings numbered 204 to 268. The boxed inset at the bottom left of this half (more Lambertville Rubber Company buildings) is a separate part.
notes: Weeden is today Weeden Street; near South Main Street the modern street runs south beside South Main Street before turning east, where the sheet draws it leaving diagonally, so its junction was hand-picked and the modern node kept.
Placed from that one hand-picked point at the atlas scale (7.85 px/ft) and the rotation of the left part (-4.7 degrees): low confidence.

Mann Co. paper mill); part 2 (right) South Main at Weeden (W. H. Gandey paper mill, Lambertville Rubber Co.); part 3 boxed inset at the bottom (Lambertville Rubber Co. sheds), unplaced. 50 ft; the sheet is turned about 19 degrees from its neighbours.

sheet-10-1.description: The left part of Sheet 10 is drawn turned on the page, with north to the left, and shows the valley of Swan Creek on the east side of Lambertville north of South Franklin Street, at 50 feet to an inch. A heavy vertical line divides it from the right part of the sheet. South Franklin Street runs along the bottom of the part with Lilly Street at the lower left corner and the foot of Swan Street below it. From South Franklin Street three roads run up the page (east): Quarry Street along a steep hillside on the left, Brunswick Avenue in the middle, and Swan Street on the right, which bends at Studdiford Avenue near the top. The creek winds between Brunswick Avenue and Swan Street in two branches that meet near South Franklin Street, and a large steep hillside fills the ground between the creek and Swan Street. Building is sparse: rows of two-storey brick and frame dwellings on both sides of Brunswick Avenue near South Franklin Street (house numbers 1 to 66 and up to 154 on the upper stretch), a few frame dwellings and sheds on Quarry Street, and scattered houses further up. Water pipes of 6 and 8 inches are drawn in Quarry Street and South Franklin Street. Block numbers 62, 63 and 64 are lettered across the part.
notes: Lilly Street is today Lily Street; Studdiford Avenue is today Studdiford Street; Quarry and Swan are Quarry Street and Swan Street.

Placed from two points along Swan Street (South Franklin Street / Swan Street detected, Studdiford Street / Swan Street hand-picked at the drawn bend): a helmert fit with no check; the fitted scale is 7.59 px/ft, 3 percent under the atlas value. Low confidence.
Brunswick Avenue / South Franklin Street and Quarry Street were not detected (the junctions lie within 20 m of each other at the lower left).

Two parts divided by a heavy vertical line: part 1 (left, turned, north to the left): Brunswick Av., Quarry, Swan, Swan Creek, S. Franklin; part 2 (right): Swan, Cottage, Lincoln Av., Douglass between Boozer and Studdiford Av. 50 ft.

sheet-10-2.description: The right part of Sheet 10 shows a newly laid-out residential tract on the east side of Lambertville, between Boozer Street on the left (west) and Studdiford Avenue on the right (east), drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the top of the page and divided from the turned left part of the sheet by a heavy vertical line. Swan Street crosses the top of the part diagonally above a narrow triangular block, block 65. Below it Cottage Street, Lincoln Avenue and Douglass Street run across the page, framing blocks 66, 67 and 68, each divided into large lots. The tract is thinly built: about a dozen two-storey frame dwellings, mostly at the lot fronts on Cottage Street, Lincoln Avenue and Douglass Street, with small stables and a poultry house. Street widths of 50 and 60 feet are marked. Below Douglass Street the ground is marked vacant beyond, and the sheet's scale of feet is printed there.
notes: Douglass is today Douglas Street; Studdiford Avenue is today Studdiford Street; Boozer, Cottage and Lincoln Avenue are Boozer Street, Cottage Street and Lincoln Avenue.
Boozer Street runs along the dividing line and Studdiford Avenue along the right edge: both are drawn with one side only, and their junctions are placed from the drawn edge.
The part is drawn at about 26 degrees from the neighbouring sheets' street grid, turned to follow its own streets.

Two parts divided by a heavy vertical line: part 1 (left, turned, north to the left): Brunswick Av., Quarry, Swan, Swan Creek, S. Franklin; part 2 (right): Swan, Cottage, Lincoln Av., Douglass between Boozer and Studdiford Av. 50 ft.

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 covers a thinly built part of eastern Lambertville on the hill above the town, between Brunswick Avenue along the top and Studdiford Avenue at the bottom. It is turned on the page, so that north lies toward the upper left, and it is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the compass rose set accordingly. Swan Street, Lincoln Avenue and Douglass Street run from top to bottom, crossed by Stryker Street, with Wayfield running off at the upper right and Cottage Street entering at the lower left. Brunswick Avenue forms the head of the sheet and then bends along the left edge, where the steep hillside is lettered Steep Hill Side. Six large blocks, numbered 69, 70, 71, 72, 73 and 74, are mostly open ground. The buildings are a scatter of detached two-storey frame dwellings with a few stables and outbuildings, strung along Swan Street, Douglass Street and the left side of Brunswick Avenue, and a larger frame dwelling with additions in the lower part of block 71 near Studdiford Avenue. A wind mill tower and a small frame house stand on the lots at the left. A note at the upper right reads that the hill sides are steep with the elevation of the crest at 130 feet, and No Exposures is lettered down the right margin. Sheet 10 is marked at the lower left edge. The street grid here is almost empty, so the fit rests on a small number of junctions.
notes: Douglass is Douglas Street today; Wayfield is not in the OpenStreetMap extract.
Stryker, Swan and Douglass are printed without a suffix; today they are Stryker Street, Swan Street and Douglas Street.
Swan Street was left out of the fit: its two junctions (with Stryker and Studdiford) carried residuals of 3 to 4.4 m while the other four fit within 1.6 m, so the modern line looks displaced.
Only 4 control points (Lincoln and Douglas against Stryker and Studdiford); Brunswick Avenue junctions were not detected.

East side, turned (rotation about -64): Brunswick Av., Studdiford Av., Swan, Lincoln Av., Stryker, Douglass, Wayfield. Swan Street left out of the fit (residuals 3 to 4.4 m); Brunswick Avenue junctions not detected; 4 points on a 2x2 grid. 50 ft.
